claims.text: Compositionally complex alloys or high-entropy alloys can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Compositionally complex alloys and high-entropy alloys have inherent resistance to temper embrittlement.
Exposure across a range of temperatures will induce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in such an alloy.
Conventional alloys undergo temper embrittlement within the proposed temperature range.
High-entropy alloys have complex, multicomponent compositions.
The complex multicomponent composition hinders the formation of embrittling phases.
The alloy composition suppresses segregation of impurities to grain boundaries.
Suppressing impurity segregation to grain boundaries prevents embrittlement.
The alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition without the dramatic loss of ductility characteristic of temper embrittlement.
Conventional alloys provide a baseline that exhibits temper embrittlement.
The exact mechanism by which compositionally complex alloys resist temper embrittlement is not fully understood.
Mechanical behavior may vary with the specific high-entropy-alloy composition.
Mechanical behavior may vary with processing history.
A Charpy impact or comparable ductility test over temperature can compare the high-entropy alloy with a conventional-alloy control.
Observation of a significant ductility loss in the high-entropy alloy over the same temperature range as the conventional alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis proposes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition while also predicting avoidance of the dramatic ductility loss that defines the asserted brittle interval; no separate criterion for brittleness is provided.
The intervention is intended to induce a brittle state, whereas the proposed mediator and mechanism are said to hinder embrittling phases and prevent embrittlement.
